title: Throughput surge mitigation via probabilistic microbatch defer and KV hotness tiering
creator: Liang Chen
description:
Problem: Under intermittent high QPS spikes (e.g., traffic bursts from PLG onboarding flows), the continuous batching controller and KV cache interactions can cause sudden GPU memory pressure, leading to elevated tail latency and token drops. Existing admission controllers use hard thresholds or percentile smoothing which can either over-throttle steady traffic or fail to react fast enough to very short-lived surges.

Goal: Implement a low-risk mitigation that reduces tail latency and GPU OOM risk during short high-QPS bursts while preserving steady-state throughput. The approach combines a lightweight probabilistic microbatch deferral heuristic at the admission layer and a KV hotness-tiering policy that temporarily compresses/evicts less-recent cache shards while protecting hot prefixes.

Scope: This ticket covers design, prototype, and a canary rollout for the admission and KV-tiering changes in the serving runtime. It does NOT include deep kernel changes or quantization work; those are follow-ups.

Key ideas: 1) Probabilistic microbatch defer: when instantaneous queue depth or token inflight rate crosses a burst threshold, each incoming request has a configurable small probability p_defer of being deferred by a short randomized backoff (e.g., 1-10 ms) to allow batching alignment without global halts. This reduces simultaneous microbatch submissions and smooths allocation spikes. 2) KV hotness tiering: maintain a light-weight per-prefix hotness estimator (decayed counters) and promote top N hot prefixes to a protected tier; non-protected prefixes become eligible for aggressive compaction/eviction and compressed storage (lower-precision or trimmed KV entries) during detected bursts. 3) Coordinated backpressure signals: admission controller emits a burst token to the KV controller to trigger temporary tier policy and reports a small set of pinned hot prefixes for protection.

Design constraints: minimal CPU overhead on request path, graceful fallback to current behavior, and ability to toggle p_defer and tier thresholds via runtime flags. Must be observable with new metrics and trace tags.

Deliverables: design doc PR, prototype change in admission controller + KV manager, e2e latency/throughput benchmark harness, canary rollout plan, dashboard with new KPIs, and an incident playbook entry.
acceptance_criteria: Canary shows >=30% reduction in 99.9th token latency spikes during synthetic short bursts (peak bursts lasting 2-5s) compared to baseline
No more than 5% reduction in median throughput during typical steady workloads
No elevated rate of incorrect / empty responses or token loss under test harness
Feature toggles are implemented and can be disabled without restarting serving processes
New metrics emitted: microbatch.defer_rate, kv.tier_eviction_rate_burst, kv.protected_prefix_count, burst_admission_trigger_count
design_notes:
Probabilistic defer parameters: default p_defer=0.12 during detected burst window; defer jitter uniform(1,8) ms. Burst detection: instantaneous token_accept_rate > baseline_rate * 2.5 or queue_depth_increment > configured delta within 100ms window. Hotness estimator: exponential decay counter per prefix with tau=30s, use top-1% by score as protected tier (configurable).

Memory safety: aggressive compaction for non-protected KV shards uses a fast best-effort serializer that reduces retention of low-utility KV entries (e.g., store only last K keys per shard). This is reversible when burst ends.

Trade-offs considered: full deterministic admission (e.g., token-bucket gating) is stricter but increases latency for many requests; probabilistic defer trades off a small expected extra latency for reduced variance and less tail pressure. Hotness-tiering requires additional metadata but avoids global KV eviction which causes higher downstream recompute cost.

Fallback plan: if novel behavior causes regressions, we will toggle p_defer=0 and revert KV-tiering to baseline evictor. Rollout gating will include automated rollback if error_rate or 99.9th latency increases by >15% over baseline.

1) Design PR: diagrams and parameter table (owner: Liang) — due 2026-02-26.
2) Admission controller prototype (owner: Marina) — implement probabilistic defer hook and burst detector; add metrics and trace tags — due 2026-03-08.
3) KV manager prototype (owner: Sandeep Rao) — implement hotness estimator and compaction API; add metrics — due 2026-03-08.
4) Bench harness: synthetic burst scenarios + real-capture replay — due 2026-03-12.
5) Internal review and safety tests — due 2026-03-16.
6) Canary rollout to 2% of serving capacity with tight telemetry — due 2026-03-20.
7) Ramp or rollback based on KPIs — finish by 2026-03-31.
testing_plan:
Unit tests for probabilistic defer on admission code, property tests to validate that defer rate matches configured p_defer under poisson arrivals, KV hotness unit tests and compaction regression tests. Load tests: replay captured high-QPS traces and run synthetic spikes (2x, 5x, 10x baseline) with 100 trial runs to measure tail behavior. Chaos tests: introduce random node latency and simulate KV serialization failures to ensure graceful fallback.

Observability: add Grafana panels for new metrics, and tracing spans for defer decisions and KV-tier actions. Ship a dashboard template for on-call.
metrics_and_rollout_gates:
Primary: 99.9th token latency (per model and per-region), burst_admission_trigger_count, microbatch.defer_rate. Safety gates: overall error rate, token drop count, GPU memory OOM count. Canary gating: no increase >10% in overall error rate and 99.9th latency improvement >=15% on targeted burst scenarios.

Automated rollback rules will be configured in the deployment job.
